JAMES M. SHELDON, JR.. OMEGA '30
^HANCELOR Lawrence A. Kimpton of
^ the University of Chicago announced
the appointment on
August 22nd of Broth
er
James M. Sheldon as assistant to the
Chancelor, a
position in which he will
coordinate the external development pro
gram of the University. He is vice-president
and director of Charles A. Stevens and
Company, Chicago loop specialty store,
with which he has been associated for
twenty-six years.
Brother Sheldon was awarded an Alumni
Citation in June in recognition of his civic
activities. Both his parents are
University
alumni. His father, a
college and law grad
uate, was one of its all-time football stars
and its only two-time football captain.
Brother Sheldon is chairman of the Cook
County Chapter of the National Founda
tion for Infantile Paralysis; member of the
Subscriptions Investigating Committee of
the Chicago Association of Commerce;
member of the Executive Committee of the
Health Division of the Chicago Welfare
Council. In 1956 he was chairman of May
or
Daley's PoHo Planning Committee. He is
a former member of the Budget Committee
of the Community Fund of Chicago. This
latter responsibility was
delegated to him a
year ago when at the height of a
rampant
upsurge of infantile paralysis in Chicago, a
drastic need was felt for guidance and a
catalystic influence among the various civic
and medical agencies concerned with
medical care for the polio stricken.
With more than a thousand victims in
the acute stages of polio requiring expert
and immediate attention, Brother Sheldon
and his team organized the limited facilities
to execute these demands. The chaos which
can so readily immobihze a fear-striken
community was thus avoided.
In Western Springs (Illinois) where he
lives at 4240 Hampton Avenue, he is presi
dent of the Park Board. Brother Sheldon
is married to the former Isabelle Hill, who
also attended the University of Chicago,
and has two daughters, Anne Boyd, a
senior at Grinnell College, and Sara, who
enters Beloit College this autumn.
By Brother Sheldon's new
leaving pri
vate enterprise to lend to educators his
proven ability to tackle problems, this
season's students and those for many sea
sons to come will benefit.
As a freshman, Jim played on the "frosh"
basketball and tennis teams. Later he
played varsity tennis.
He dropped out of college for one
year
to learn by experience what he sought in
later life in the business world and also
to visit Europe. Interestingly, on the trip
going abroad he met a
charming girl, one
Isabelle Hill, who today is Mrs. James
Sheldon, Jr.
Jim rounded out his college days by
serving as freshman trainer for the House
and later held important offices as one of
the Omega chapter executives. After grad
uation Jim's career in the business world
proved that he had gotten a valuable back
ground from his idea cif how to spend his
college days.
Today, however, the challenge of his
opportunity to serve as one of the leaders
building anew a
great university to cope
with the educational demands of his gener
ation is the major interest in this Omega
man's life. Basing our belief upon his past,
we
may feel confident that James M.
Sheldon, Jr., Omega '30, will contribute
largely to that crusade.

THE CONVENTION STORY
By John H. Caldwell, III, Psi '58, and Thomas K. Kunichika, Psi '58
UNDERGRADUATE
and alumni mem
bers from every chapter of the Frater
nity met at the Psi chapter, Hamilton Col
lege, Clinton, New York, on the fifth and
sixth of September for the 115th Conven
tion of Psi Upsilon, held in the 124th year
of the Fraternity. Approximately 170
Brethren were
present at various times
throughout the Convention.
It seems to us at the Psi that before we
recount the events of the Convention, it
would be appropriate for us to express our
gratitude to those who helped make the
Convention possible and a success. To
Brothers Horace Seely-Brown, Jr., Psi, '29,
and Russell S. Callow, Theta Theta '16, we
are
especially indebted. These two Broth
ers, who were
generous enough to address
the Convention at the dinner meetings on
Thursday and Friday evenings, added
much to the Convention, giving freely of
their own time. To President Robert W.
McEwen of Hamilton College, we
give
thanks for his address of welcome at the
opening session of the Convention. To
Brother Paul B. Williams, Psi '08, we
give
thanks for graciously consenting to be
toastmaster on
Friday evening. Brother
Edward T. Richards, Sigma '27, receives
our
gratitude for his invaluable aid in mak
ing arrangements for the favors. We thank
Brothers Gardner A. Callanen, Jr., Psi '29,
and Albert G. Hazelden, Psi '24, without
whose aid the active Chapter would never
have been able to organize the Convention.
And to all the Psi Alumni who gave sup
port, and all the delegates of the Chapters
who attended, we
give special thanks, for
without them the Convention would have
never taken place. Finally, to the members
of the Executive Council, without whose
guidance and advice, we would have been
unable to properly plan for the Convention,
we
give heartfelt thanks.

The activities of the Convention were
by
no means limited to the business sessions.
The evenings were set aside for banqueting

nity situation at Hamilton and the relative

torical nature of the Fraternity, stressing

ment in the social history of the United

which time the early business assembly
convened in the chemistry auditorium on

ing, at approximately 12:00 M., the dele
gates returned to the Chapter House. Tak
ing advantage of the typically beautiful
fall day, most of the delegates strolled
through the campus and headed "down
hill" to the House. Awaiting all at the
Chapter House was an
enticing buffet
luncheon, prepared under the direction of
the Psi's able cook, Casper Pliseck, and

the pleasant weather, many delegates ate
at the several tables set up on the porch.
Following the conclusion of the luncheon
about 1:30, everyone moved to the back
lawn of the House for the official conven
tion photograph. After a short period of in
evitable squirming, the picture was suc
cessfully completed, and the delegates
returned to the chemistry auditorium for

left the Chapter House for Twin Ponds

demic Standing and Awards, presented the

ing to the delegates of the Epsilon Phi

well stressed the meaning of the Conven
tion to the host Chapter. Besides serving to

pendence of the Chapter upon its alumni.
Brother Williams then introduced the
main speaker of the evening Russell (Rusty)

lengthy ovation.
After the applause, a few of the older
brothers took early leave, while others,
more
sprightly, sealed the past two days'
friendships with barstool conversations.
Summary
The interest, energy, and competence of
the delegates made the business sessions of
the Convention hvely and profitable. From
the social and business events of the
Convention, emerged friendships which
strengthened the national unity of the fra
ternity. Besides the warmth of fellowship

days, the Convention proved the Frater
nity a
nationally unified organization, not a
mere loose aggregation of Chapters. As
each Brother left the Psi, he sensed, besides
a
physical contentment, a

sciousness of the real meaning of Psi Upsi
lon Brotherhood.

CHALLENGE TO HISTORY
Address Delivered at Thursday Convention Dinner
By Thomas K. Kunichika
Psi '58
Because history, by definition, is the ac
count of things past, it is difficult to say with
any great accuracy that any report in history
is entirely accurate. We can
only use what the
contemporaries of a
particular age have writ
ten for our information. And even these
recorders do not agree.
To illustrate this last point, let me tell you
of an
experience of mine early this summer.
I received in early June a note�a most dis
concerting note�initialled E.D.B. It started
off, "Dear Kunichika," (there is nothing quite
as
disconcerting as
any communication that
starts off like that�how would you like to get
a note that started "Dear Kunichika"?). This
is what was in the rest of the note: "Is open
to confusion, however, the Convention of
1858, p. 360 Annals "officially" named that
convention the twenty-fifth, and that has con
tinued for the 100 years! It might be more
confusing to change now, for you would need
many years to avoid dupHcation!"
The E.D.B. is Earl D. Babst, former presi
dent of the Executive Council to whom even
the venerable Weed would bow. Moreover,
Brother Babst wrote the particular article on
convention which appears in the Annals.
There was
very Uttle I could do except
check the Annals and our own records of the
1858 Convention. I guess our records disagree
with Brother Babst's or the recorders of that
Convention (the records are all written in
long hand) disagreed, for our records mention
nothing about giving that convention a
specific
numerical name. The indication for number
ing comes the next year, 1859, when the Con
vention was called the Twenty-sixth Annual
Convention of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity.
This all illustrates that history is recorded
differently, even
by contemporaries of a
given
period.
The Psi was chartered in 1843. At the time.
there were two other societies on the Hill�
Sigma Phi and the mother house of Alpha
Delta Phi. Both had been on the HiU over
ten years by the time the Psi was chartered.
But let me read you a few Unes from the His
tory of the Psi which was started in 1847.
The History says, "Both had, as a direct
result of long and uninterrupted prosperity,
become corrupted by a thousand and one acts
of injustice. But a
change was at hand. The
desolating influence of 'the Harlot' was soon
to be crippled. A wise providence had ordered
that Purity and Innocence should rise and
combat the mother of iniquity."
Thus was born the Psi�mothered by purity
and innocence. Well, I'm not so sure that all
was as
pure and as irmocent as the History
would lead us to believe. In fact, no end of
conniving went into operation once contact
with the Beta and Theta was made.
A long series of midnight meetings, secret
agreements, and throat slashing started. Be
sides the high intellectual aims and virtues
of the fraternities was the penchant of fra
ternity men in those days to steal all the
secrets of other societies. Each claimed to be
pure and claimed an abhorrence of secrecy.
So, for insurance, they all tried to learn the
others' secrets to keep theirs from being made
pubhc.
At a time when fraternities were somewhat
different (I think I can
safely say that), knowl
edge of the secrets of others was a definite
threat to fraternity men. Thus we have what
we call the Account of Alpha Delta Phi (and
I think we have to thank the Gamma chapter
of an earlier time for it) written by Samuel
Eells, founder of Alpha Delt, in our records.
I cannot begin to go into the actual history
of the Psi. It is both too long and, to many,
somewhat tiring. But if any of you are in
terested, I'd be glad to speak to you later. At
the risk of sounding preachy, I would Hke to
say this, if any of you are
history majors like
myself and are interested in American social
history, and if you have the gumption to wade
through all the papers in your respective
archives, I should say, give it a
try. The
history you will read will not be the history
of the fraternity only; it will be the history
of your college and also partly the social his
tory of America. It can be fascinating, and
who knows what kind of a skeleton you might
dig up?

POLITICS NO "DIRTY WORD"
Editorial from the Utica Observer-Dispatch of September 7, 1957
Rep. Horace Seely-Brown (R-Conn.) gives
testimony "politics is not a
dirty word" and
"there is nothing wrong with being a
poli
tician."
While the word "politics" has a doubtful
connation when often used, it is also true the
country needs politicians. Political experts are
required to make the laws, see that they
operate equitably and improve self-govern
ment forms. But there is, of course, a differ
ence in politicians.
As often expounded, when the abler people
refuse to help run tlieir own affairs�go into
politics�then they will have to take the rules
laid down by the willing politicians, who may
be venal, self-serving or
just simply dumb in
some cases instead of public-spirited.
That's why Seely-Brown, who is a native
of Chnton and a son of a former professor
at Hamilton College, urged his hearers at the
124th annual convention of Psi Upsilon na
tional fraternity on the Hill to accept politics
as a
part of the daily responsibility of every
citizen.
He said "even though many estimable
citizens shrink from any association with poli
tics by classifying themselves as
'independents'
or
by making the mistake of supporting socalled 'non-partisan' local governments in their
communities, the fact is that politics and
politicians are an essential part of our
system
of government.
"One of the things of greatest value that
you can
carry back home," he told his collegetrained audience, "is that there is nothing
wrong with being a
politician, in fact that
you should aspire to be one, to the extent
that your time and talents permit."
We're not sure the boys in the back room
or the brain trusts of Little City Hall approve
too many brains getting into politics, but
Seely-Brown is right that more of them
ought to do so. Our city, county, village,
town and state governments attract too little
attention from the men who have talents to
provide better government than we have.

[To the best of the Editors' knowledge, most members of the Fraternity have never had an
opportunity to read the formal Chapter Reports which are submitted at our National Conventions.
In view of the fact that The Diamond is now
published on a
quarterly basis of Spring, Summer,
Fall and Winter, it is thought that we should give our readers the opportunity of seeing these
reports so that they may have a
full year's review of their own
Chapters and such other Chapters
as
may be of special interest to them.
In the limited time of a
two-day Convention, it is possible to read only a
very few of the thirty
Chapter Reports. The Diamond, however, reaching as it does over two-thirds of our member
ship, makes it possible for all of these reports to receive wide circulation in the Fraternity.

THETA Union College
The Theta chapter of Psi Upsilon started
off the year with a successful rushing pro
gram headed by Edward V. Ince, then Presi
dent of the House, and Sheldon P. French,
Chairman of the Rushing Committee. At the
close of the formal rushing period, we
pledged
ten men, one of whom left college at the
end of the first semester because of bad marks
and one other depledged when be got married.
These two men were
replaced by the pledg
ing of two more men at the beginning of the
second semester. We feel we were selective
in our choice of whom we bid, and, as a result,
we obtained some of the top men in the
freshman class.
The Theta was more active in sporfs this
year than it has been for a
long time. We
were
represented on almost every varsity
squad on
campus.
In social activities, we feel that the Theta
showed itself as a
leading fraternity on
campus. The season, which included the
usual football parties and three College-spon
sored weekends, was climaxed by a formal
cocktail party for the faculty, at the begiiming
of May.
Academically, the Theta has not done so
well. Only three members of the house made
the Dean's List. While others in the house
have obtained marks equal to and above the
college all men's average, we still have too
many brothers whose marks put them in bad
standing with the college. We have been
confronted with this problem of scholarship
for a number of years now. The house trustees
have met with the house officers on numerous
occasions to see what could be done to raise
the scholastic standing of the Theta, but so far
no one has come
up with a
positive solution
to the problem. Various study rules have been
initiated with some success, but they have not
produced a definite effect on
raising the house
average. Both the house and the trustees have
shown concern over the matter, and the only
